citation: Longmuir, P. E., Woodruff, S. J., Boyer, C., Lloyd, M., & Tremblay, M. S. (2018). Physical Literacy Knowledge Questionnaire: Feasibility, validity, and reliability for Canadian children aged 8 to 12 years. BMC Public Health, 18. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-018-5890-y

key_findings:
The relative age effect (RAE) bias in CAPL scores was generally negligible, although some differences in physical competence (e.g., muscular strength and height) were observed for children born earlier in the year.
Boys and girls born in the first three months showed slightly higher scores in certain domains but with minimal effect sizes.
RAE bias had limited practical significance on overall CAPL scores.

citation: Robinson, D. B., & Randall, L. (2017). Marking Physical Literacy or Missing the Mark on Physical Literacy? A Conceptual Critique of Canada’s Physical Literacy Assessment Instruments. Meas. Phys. Educ. Exerc. Sci., 21(1), 40–55. https://doi.org/10.1080/1091367X.2016.1249793

citation: Corbin, C. B. (2016). Implications of Physical Literacy for Research and Practice: A Commentary. Res. Q. Exerc. Sport, 87(1), 14–27. https://doi.org/10.1080/02701367.2016.1124722

citation: Demian, M. N., Jean Shapiro, R., & Thornton, W. L. (2016). An observational study of health literacy and medication adherence in adult kidney transplant recipients. Clin. Kidney J., 9(6), 858–865. https://doi.org/10.1093/ckj/sfw076
key_findings: Lower health literacy was associated with poorer immunosuppressant adherence. The study highlights the need for interventions that enhance health literacy to improve adherence

citation: Milne, R. A., Puts, M. T. E., Papadakos, J., Le, L. W., Milne, V. C., Hope, A. J., Catton, P., & Giuliani, M. E. (2015). Predictors of High eHealth Literacy in Primary Lung Cancer Survivors. J. Cancer Educ., 30(4), 685–692. https://doi.org/10.1007/s13187-014-0744-5
key_findings:
Only 33.7% of survivors perceived themselves as having high eHealth literacy.
Significant predictors of high eHealth literacy included:
Access to eResources (96% in high eHealth group vs. 69% in low eHealth group, p=0.004).
Higher education (79% with post-secondary education in high eHealth group vs. 44% in low eHealth group, p=0.003).
No significant associations were found between eHealth literacy and age, gender, marital status, or HRQoL.
Survivors often lacked confidence in evaluating online health information and using it for health decisions, highlighting a digital divide.

citation: Oliffe, J. L., Hannan-Leith, M. N., Ogrodniczuk, J. S., Black, N., Mackenzie, C. S., Lohan, M., & Creighton, G. (2016). Men’s depression and suicide literacy: a nationally representative Canadian survey. J. Ment. Health, 25(6), 520–526. https://doi.org/10.1080/09638237.2016.1177770
key_findings:
Respondents correctly answered 67.1% of D-Lit items and 53.7% of LOSS items, indicating limited mental health literacy.
Females demonstrated higher literacy than males for both depression and suicide topics.
Common misconceptions included depressive symptoms and suicide risk factors, such as incorrectly linking depression to multiple personalities or misjudging the impact of discussing suicidal thoughts.
The study advocates for gender-sensitive public health campaigns to improve mental health literacy and address stigma.

citation: Mcluckie, A., Kutcher, S., Wei, Y., & Weaver, C. (2014). Sustained improvements in students’ mental health literacy with use of a mental health curriculum in Canadian schools. BMC Psychiatry, 14(1). https://doi.org/10.1186/s12888-014-0379-4
key_findings:
Knowledge: Scores increased significantly post-intervention (from a mean of 14.91 to 18.55, p < 0.001) and were sustained at follow-up (mean 18.22, p < 0.001).
Attitudes: Modest but significant improvements post-intervention (mean increased from 34.09 to 35.34, p < 0.001) and maintained at follow-up (mean 34.26, p = 0.007).
Embedding mental health literacy into the regular school curriculum positively impacted students' knowledge and attitudes, providing a scalable model for stigma reduction and mental health promotion.

citation: Yamashita, T., & Kunkel, S. R. (2015). key_findings: Literacy skills mediated the effect of education on health in all study locations, but the degree of mediation varied. For instance, numeracy skills in the United States and prose literacy skills in Italy were stronger predictors of health outcomes.

citation: Jia, F., Gottardo, A., Koh, P. W., Chen, X., & Pasquarella, A. (2014). The role of acculturation in reading a second language: Its relation to english literacy skills in immigrant chinese adolescents. Read. Res. Q., 49(2), 251–261. https://doi.org/10.1002/rrq.69
key_findings:
Mainstream acculturation significantly predicted English reading comprehension even after controlling for vocabulary, word decoding, and length of residence in Canada.
Heritage enculturation had no significant relationship with English reading skills.
Cognitive-linguistic factors (vocabulary and word reading skills) explained most of the variance in reading comprehension, but sociocultural factors added unique contributions.

citation: Gong, Z., Haig, S. L., Pope, J. E., Rohekar, S., Rohekar, G., LeRiche, N. G. H., & Thompson, A. E. (2015). Health literacy rates in a population of patients with rheumatoid arthritis in Southwestern Ontario. J. Rheumatol., 42(9), 1610–1615. https://doi.org/10.3899/jrheum.141509
key_findings:
Rates of low health literacy ranged from 14.1% to 18.6% across the tests.

citation: Lupattelli, A., Picinardi, M., Einarson, A., & Nordeng, H. (2014). Health literacy and its association with perception of teratogenic risks and health behavior during pregnancy. Patient Educ. Couns., 96(2), 171–178. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.pec.2014.04.014
key_findings:
Low-health literacy women:
Reported higher perceived risks for medications (e.g., penicillin and swine flu vaccine).
Demonstrated more negative beliefs about medications during pregnancy.
Had higher rates of non-adherence to prescribed medications (25% vs. 19.2% for high-health literacy women).
Risk perception and beliefs about medications mediated the relationship between health literacy and medication adherence.
Policy implication: Clinicians should account for patients' health literacy levels to promote better adherence during pregnancy.

citation: Landry, R., Minor-Corriveau, M., & Bélanger, R. (2015). Is student achievement on standardized EQAO testing reflected in their annual academic performance?: A longitudinal study. Int. J. Literacies, 22(4), 1–26. https://doi.org/10.18848/2327-0136/cgp/v22i04/1-26
key_findings:
Strong correlations were found between classroom grades and EQAO results in some cases, especially for reading and writing, but not for oral communication.
Girls consistently outperformed boys in literacy measures.
Students whose dominant language was French performed better than those whose dominant language was English, though this gap decreased by grade 6.
The correlations for students with IEPs were weaker, highlighting challenges in aligning classroom and standardized assessments for this group.
The study raised questions about the validity of EQAO tests for students with different linguistic and educational backgrounds.

citation: Mikhail, D., Visscher, K. L., Chen, N., Wang, J., Emara, B. Y., & Hutnik, C. M. (2015). Patient-appropriate health literacy educational materials in ophthalmology. Can. J. Ophthalmol., 50(1), 19–25. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jcjo.2014.08.002
key_findings:

Patients comprehended and preferred materials written at a grade 5 reading level with illustrations, as opposed to grade 10 level materials.
Participants spent significantly less time reading the grade 5 level pamphlet but achieved higher comprehension scores.
Patients reported that lower-level pamphlets were easier to read and understand.
The study supports using lower-literacy materials universally to improve patient understanding and satisfaction.

citation: Bourgoin, R. (2014). The predictive effects of L1 and L2 early literacy indicators on reading in French immersion. Can. Mod. Lang. Rev., 70(3), 355–380. https://doi.org/10.3138/cmlr.2346
key_findings:
Kindergarten L1 predictors (e.g., Letter Naming) strongly correlated with L2 reading outcomes in Grade 3.

Cross-linguistic transfer of literacy skills, particularly alphabetic knowledge, is crucial for predicting L2 reading abilities.

citation: Longmuir, P. E., Boyer, C., Lloyd, M., Yang, Y., Boiarskaia, E., Zhu, W., & Tremblay, M. S. (2015). The Canadian Assessment of Physical Literacy: Methods for children in grades 4 to 6 (8 to 12 years). BMC Public Health, 15(1). https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-015-2106-6
key_findings:

Boys generally scored higher in physical competence and engagement in physical activity, while girls showed a decline in motivation at age 11 but recovered by age 12.
Teacher ratings positively correlated with CAPL scores, supporting validity.
Findings suggest the need for targeted interventions to support physical literacy in girls and other groups.

citation: Zibrik, L., Khan, S., Bangar, N., Stacy, E., Novak Lauscher, H., & Ho, K. (2015). citation: Mardhani-Bayne, A., & Shamchuk, L. (2022). Early Literacy Learning for Future Library Paraprofessionals: Authentic Learning in Library Education. Partnership: The Canadian Journal of Library & Information Practice & Research, 17(2), 1–20. https://doi.org/10.21083/partnership.v17i2.6808

Hands-on course elements (e.g., guest speakers, creating virtual storytime programs) were identified as significant contributors to learning.

The use of authentic learning elements, such as practical assignments and real-world applications, enhanced the students' readiness for professional roles.

citation: Rodriguez, C., CAIRNEY, J., VELDHUIZEN, S., GRAHAM, J. D., BEDARD, C., BREMER, E., & KRIELLAARS, D. (2018). A Construct Validation Study of PLAYfun. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise, 50(4), 855–862.

citation: Rose, K. (2017). Assessing Changes in Scientific Literacy in an Alberta Science Option Course: Myth-Busting Science 25. Alberta Science Education Journal, 45(1), 11–20.

Children scored at age norms for English reading comprehension and decoding but below norms for English and Chinese receptive vocabulary.
HLE factors positively influenced Chinese receptive vocabulary but showed no significant correlation with English literacy skills.

Parent-child shared reading and the number of Chinese books at home were key predictors of Chinese receptive vocabulary.

citation: Tighe, E. L. (2014). Broadening Our Perspectives on Adult Literacy, Numeracy, and Problem-Solving Skills with PIAAC Data: A Commentary on The Centre for Literacy’s 2014 Summer Institute. Journal of Research & Practice for Adult Literacy, Secondary & Basic Education, 3(3), 63–69.

The findings highlight the need for enhanced educational strategies and interventions, particularly in numeracy and problem-solving skills.

citation: ERCIKAN, K., ROTH, W.-M., & ASIL, M. (2015). Cautions About Inferences From International Assessments: The Case of PISA 2009. Teachers College Record, 117(1), 1–28.

citation: Beks, T. A., Cairns, S. L., Smygwaty, S. L., Osorio, O. A. L. M., & Hill, S. J. (2018). Counsellor-in-Residence: Evaluation of a Residence-Based Initiative to Promote Student Mental Health. Canadian Journal of Higher Education, 48(2), 55–73.

citation: Krupar, A., Horvatek, R., & Byun, S. (2017). Does Nonformal Education Matter? Nonformal Education, Immigration, and Skills in Canada. Adult Education Quarterly, 67(3), 186–208.

On-the-job training was the most impactful type of NFE, associated with higher skill outcomes.
Policy implications include expanding access to NFE programs for immigrants to support integration and skill development.

citation: Lodewyk, K. R., & Mandigo, J. L. (2017). Early Validation Evidence of a Canadian Practitioner-Based Assessment of Physical Literacy in Physical Education: Passport for Life. Physical Educator, 74(3), 441–475.

Students demonstrated better understanding of physical literacy concepts post-assessment.
The tool was deemed suitable for formative use in educational settings.

citation: Lodewyk, K. R. (2019). Early Validation Evidence of the Canadian Practitioner-Based Assessment of Physical Literacy in Secondary Physical Education. Physical Educator, 76(3), 634–660.

citation: Glithero, L. (Diz). (2021). Evaluating Ocean Perceptions and Ocean Values: The Canadian Ocean Literacy Survey. Canadian Journal of Environmental Education, 24(1), 216–232.

citation: Cummins, P. A., Harrington, A. K., & Yamashita, T. (2022). Individual Learning Accounts: A Comparison of Implemented and Proposed Initiatives. Adult Learning, 33(4), 147–157.
key_findings:
Adults with low literacy skills participate in AET at significantly lower rates compared to those with medium or high skills.
Participation rates for low-skilled adults ranged from 20% (France) to 38% (England), while those with medium or high skills ranged from 40% (France) to 65% (United States).
Barriers to AET for low-skilled adults include financial costs, institutional challenges, and dispositional factors (e.g., lack of self-confidence).
Effective AET financing models must provide adequate funding, simplify access, and ensure program quality to address situational and institutional barriers.
Low-skilled adults benefit from support structures like counseling, tutoring, childcare, and transportation.
Examples of funding models (e.g., training vouchers, individual savings accounts) showed varying levels of success across the countries studied.

citation: Cheng, L., & Sun, Y. (2015). Interpreting the Impact of the Ontario Secondary School Literacy Test on Second Language Students Within an Argument-Based Validation Framework. Language Assessment Quarterly, 12(1), 50–66.

citation: Jungwee Park. (2022). JOB MISMATCHES AMONG INDIGENOUS WORKERS IN CANADA: FINDINGS FROM PIAAC DATA. Canadian Journal of Native Studies, 41(1), 23–48.

Indigenous workers were more likely to be under-skilled and less likely to be over-skilled compared to non-Indigenous workers.

Part-time Indigenous workers were more likely to be over-educated and over-skilled, while self-employed workers were more likely to be under-educated but not under-skilled.

Job satisfaction was higher among under-skilled Indigenous workers but lower among over-educated workers.

citation: Vézina, S., & Bélanger, A. (2020). Literacy Skills as an Explanation for Labor Market Imbalances by Occupational Type in Canada: Microsimulation Projections for 2014–2024. Population Research & Policy Review, 39(6), 1019–1049.

Omitting literacy from workforce projections leads to an overestimation of workers in management and high-skilled positions and underestimation in lower-skilled jobs.
Immigrants with higher literacy skills are more likely to hold skilled jobs, yet disparities in management roles persist.
Accounting for literacy results in better-aligned labor supply and demand projections, revealing gaps in overqualification attributable to literacy deficits

citation: Volante, L., Klinger, D., Bilgili, Ö., & Siegel, M. (2017). Making Sense of the Performance (Dis)advantage for Immigrant Students Across Canada. Canadian Journal of Education / Revue Canadienne de l’Éducation, 40(3), 329–361.

citation: Hillier, C., Zarifa, D., & Hango, D. (2022). Mind the Gaps: Examining Youth’s Reading, Math and Science Skills Across Northern and Rural Canada*. Rural Sociology, 87(1), 264–302.

Southern youth outperform northern youth in mathematics skills.
Urban youth (southern and northern) show advantages in reading proficiencies compared to their rural counterparts.
In science literacy, urban youth (both southern and northern) outperform rural northern youth.
Socioeconomic factors, parenting styles, and academic aspirations contribute to but do not fully explain regional skill disparities.
Implications highlight the need for tailored policies to address skill gaps in northern and rural Canada.

citation: Hagerman, M., Beach, P., Cotnam-Kappel, M., & Hébert, C. (2020). Multiple Perspectives on Digital Literacies Research Methods in Canada. International Journal of E-Learning & Distance Education, 35(1), 1–38.
key_findings: The document is a theoretical and methodological exploration, proposing that research in digital literacies needs to account for complex, real-time interactions and should be deeply embedded in the specific cultural, linguistic, and educational contexts of Canadian society.

citation: Park, J., & Fallon, G. (2016). NOTIONS OF LITERACY IN THE K-12 SCHOOL SYSTEM IN BRITISH COLUMBIA EDUCATION SINCE 2002: A CONTESTED TERRAIN. Canadian Journal of Educational Administration & Policy, 179, 1–38.
key_findings:
The tension between autonomous and ideological literacy models in policy and practice.

There is a need to redefine literacy to include broader competencies for sociocultural and political change.
The emphasis on standardized testing oversimplifies literacy and fails to address community-specific needs.

citation: St. Clair, R. (2016). Plus ça change - The failure of PIAAC to drive evidence-based policy in Canada. Report: Zeitschrift Für Weiterbildungsforschung, 39(2), 225–239. https://search.ebscohost.com/login.aspx?direct=true&db=eue&AN=118193399&site=ehost-live

citation: Elias, P. V. (2023). Race, ethnicity, and literacy and Essential Skills in Canada. Journal of Vocational Education & Training, 75(1), 43–62.

citation: Briere, J. L., & Wilson, J. R. (2018). Reading Ability and Multiliteracy among Rural Saskatchewan High School Students. Journal of Literacy & Technology, 19(2), 99–127.

citation: Woods-McConney, A., Oliver, M. C., McConney, A., Schibeci, R., & Maor, D. (2014). Science Engagement and Literacy: A retrospective analysis for students in Canada and Australia. International Journal of Science Education, 36(10), 1588–1608.

citation: Syrnyk, C., McArthur, A., Zwack, A., & Handelsman, A. (2023). Supporting Young Readers: A Mixed-Methods Study of Their Literacy, Behaviour, and Perceptions When Reading Aloud to Dogs or Adults. Early Childhood Education Journal, 51(6), 1091–1105.
